idioms.meaning: to be sad about something that can't be changed
idioms.whenToUse: When a small mistake already happened and worrying won't help.
idioms.literalNote: There may be no milk; it means don't worry about the past.
fallbackExamples: It's broken now. No use crying over spilled milk.
Don't cry over spilled milk – just try again.
She lost the game but didn't cry over spilled milk.

idioms.meaning: something extra that makes a good thing even better
idioms.whenToUse: When a good day gets one more nice surprise.
idioms.literalNote: It is not about real cake; it means "an extra good thing".
fallbackExamples: The free dessert was the icing on the cake.
Good weather was the icing on the cake.
Meeting the chef was the icing on the cake.

idioms.meaning: to relax after stress by doing something active
idioms.whenToUse: When you exercise or shout to feel less stressed.
idioms.literalNote: You are not a train; it means relaxing after stress.
fallbackExamples: I go running to let off steam after work.
The kids let off steam at the park.
Dancing helps me let off steam.

idioms.meaning: to decide as things happen, without a plan
idioms.whenToUse: When plans are not fixed and you will decide later.
idioms.literalNote: No music is needed; it means deciding later.
fallbackExamples: Let's play it by ear and see the weather.
We didn't book a hotel; we played it by ear.
I'm not sure about Saturday. Let's play it by ear.

idioms.meaning: to say no now but yes another time
idioms.whenToUse: When you can't accept an invitation today but want to later.
idioms.literalNote: There is no rain; it means "maybe another time".
fallbackExamples: Can I take a rain check on dinner tonight?
She took a rain check on the movie.
I'm tired. Can I take a rain check?

idioms.meaning: just in time; at the last moment
idioms.whenToUse: When you arrive or finish just before it is too late.
idioms.literalNote: "Nick" is not a person; it means the last moment.
fallbackExamples: We caught the train in the nick of time.
The doctor arrived in the nick of time.
I finished my homework in the nick of time.

idioms.meaning: a very small amount compared to what is needed
idioms.whenToUse: When something helps only a tiny bit.
idioms.literalNote: It is not about real water; it means "very small".
fallbackExamples: Ten dollars is a drop in the bucket for rent.
Our donation is a drop in the bucket, but it helps.
One tree is a drop in the bucket.

idioms.meaning: to become organized and do things well
idioms.whenToUse: When someone needs to stop being messy or lazy.
idioms.literalNote: It is not about acting; it means getting organized.
fallbackExamples: I need to get my act together before the exam.
He finally got his act together and found a job.
Get your act together – the guests arrive at six.

idioms.meaning: too old to do something (said as a joke)
idioms.whenToUse: When people joke about getting older, like on a birthday.
idioms.literalNote: No real hill; it is a joke about age.
fallbackExamples: My brother turned 40 and says he's over the hill.
You're not over the hill – you're 35!
He joked that he was over the hill at the gym.

idioms.spoken: up to my ears in work
idioms.meaning: very busy with too much of something
idioms.whenToUse: When you have too much work, bills or tasks.
idioms.literalNote: You are not underwater; it means "too much".
fallbackExamples: I'm up to my ears in homework this week.
She is up to her ears in wedding plans.
We're up to our ears in boxes after moving.

idioms.meaning: to accept the bad results of your actions
idioms.whenToUse: When someone must deal with trouble they caused.
idioms.literalNote: There is no music; it means accepting the consequences.
fallbackExamples: He broke the window, so now he must face the music.
I forgot to pay; time to face the music.
She faced the music and told her boss the truth.

idioms.meaning: a topic that is difficult and people avoid
idioms.whenToUse: When a subject causes arguments, like politics or money.
idioms.literalNote: It is not about food; it means a difficult topic.
fallbackExamples: Rent control is a hot potato in the city.
Nobody wanted to talk about the hot potato.
The new rule became a hot potato at work.

idioms.meaning: to just manage, usually with money or work
idioms.whenToUse: When you have just enough to survive a hard time.
idioms.literalNote: You are not swimming; it means just surviving.
fallbackExamples: With two jobs, I keep my head above water.
The small shop is keeping its head above water.
She kept her head above water during the busy season.

idioms.meaning: a person who watches a lot of TV and doesn't move much
idioms.whenToUse: When you joke about someone who is lazy at home.
idioms.literalNote: It is not about food; it means a lazy TV watcher.
fallbackExamples: On Sundays, I'm a total couch potato.
My cat is a couch potato.
Don't be a couch potato – let's go for a walk.

idioms.meaning: to be the person who makes decisions
idioms.whenToUse: When someone is the boss or in control.
idioms.literalNote: Nobody shoots; it means making decisions.
fallbackExamples: At home, my wife calls the shots.
Who calls the shots in this office?
She calls the shots on the project.

idioms.meaning: both people are responsible in a problem
idioms.whenToUse: When an argument or problem is caused by two people.
idioms.literalNote: No dancing is needed; it means both are responsible.
fallbackExamples: Don't blame only him – it takes two to tango.
It takes two to tango in any argument.
They both made mistakes; it takes two to tango.
